568.title: Six leaks
568.hook: wealth drains through drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness
568.carry: too hot, too late, too tired
568.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often teach the Sigalovada's six leaks to lay people as practical household advice, and Buddhist economics writers cite it alongside the sutta's advice on saving and sharing wealth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four motives, desire, hate, delusion and fear. Your line: desire, hate, delusion, or fear? Today the Buddha talks to Sigala about money.

Open a banking app and look at last month. There's usually no single disaster. Just a lot of small drips: a subscription you forgot, takeout three nights running, a late-night purchase you can't quite remember making. The money didn't explode. It leaked. The Buddha, talking to a young householder in a world with no apps, names the same thing: six openings through which a household's wealth drains away.
screen: `NO DISASTER, JUST DRIPS.` → `A YOUNG HOUSEHOLDER'S BUDGET.` → `SIX OPENINGS.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is apayamukha, literally a mouth or opening toward loss. The six: drinking intoxicants, roaming the streets at the wrong hours, haunting fairs and shows, gambling, keeping bad company, and idleness. For each one, the Buddha lists six dangers, and the details are wonderfully specific. Gambling: the winner makes enemies, the loser mourns what he lost, his money is gone, his word isn't trusted when he speaks in public, his friends look down on him, and nobody wants him to marry into their family. Roaming at night: he leaves himself unprotected, and his family and property too, he's suspected of crimes, and rumors attach to him. And idleness has the best list of all. The idle man doesn't work, saying: it's too cold. It's too hot. It's too late. It's too early. I'm too hungry. I'm too full. Every reason sounds reasonable. That's what makes it a leak. This isn't a sermon against pleasure, and he isn't asking a householder to live like a monk. Elsewhere in the same sutta he tells him to enjoy part of his wealth. He's simply pointing to where it goes when you're not watching. And the leaks aren't only money. Each one drains time, health, trust and friendships too. None of them is dramatic. It's one more drink, one more night out, one more too late, too early.
screen: `APAYAMUKHA: OPENINGS TO LOSS.` · `SIX LEAKS, SIX DANGERS EACH.` · `TOO COLD, TOO HOT, TOO LATE.` · `NOT A SERMON AGAINST PLEASURE.` · then, large: `SIX LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Look honestly at your own week, without blame, and ask where something leaks: money, yes, but also time, energy, attention. Let the most ordinary leak come to mind, and picture the moment it usually happens: the evening, the phone, the excuse. Breathe with it, and picture plugging it, just once.
Six leaks. In DN 31 the six openings through which wealth drains: drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness. Today's word.
Your line: too hot, too late, too tired. Small drips, not disasters. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

569.title: The true friend
569.hook: false friends and true friends, and how to tell them apart
569.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers teach the Sigalovada's eight kinds of friend to young people and families, and the Buddha's wider teaching calls good friendship, kalyanamittata, the whole of the holy life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six leaks, the ways wealth drains away. Your line: too hot, too late, too tired. One leak was bad company, and today the Buddha tells Sigala how to spot it.

Moving day. You've asked around: anyone free Saturday? One friend sends ten heart emojis and a long message about how much they wish they could. One says they'll be there, then asks to borrow your car next week. One goes quiet. And one just shows up at eight with coffee and a dolly, and stays until the last box is in. The Sigalovada has a name for every one of them.
screen: `ANYONE FREE SATURDAY?` → `HEARTS, FAVORS, SILENCE.` → `ONE SHOWS UP AT EIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells Sigala, there are four who look like friends and aren't. The taker gives little and asks a lot, and helps only out of fear or for his own gain. The talker is all words: generous about the past and the future, but when you need something now, he points to his bad luck. The flatterer agrees with whatever you do, good or bad, praises you to your face, and runs you down behind your back. And the companion in wasting is your partner for drinking, roaming at night, shows and gambling. Then four true friends. The helper looks after you when you're careless, guards your things, is a refuge when you're afraid, and when there's a job to do, gives you twice what you asked for. The one who's the same in good times and bad tells you his secrets, keeps yours, doesn't leave you when things go wrong, and would give his life for you. The one who points the way keeps you from wrong, encourages what's good, tells you what you haven't heard, and points out the way to heaven. And the one who cares doesn't celebrate your bad luck, is glad at your good luck, stops others when they speak ill of you, and praises those who speak well of you. Every test is something you can watch for. And there's a mirror in it: the same list tells you what kind of friend to be.

570.title: East and south
570.hook: parents and children, teachers and students: duties both ways
570.carry: respect flows up, care flows down
570.howItsDone: In some Buddhist countries children bow to their parents and students to their teachers at festivals such as Thailand's teacher-honoring ceremony, and families make offerings and merit in memory of parents who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four false friends and four true ones. Your line: the friend in need. Today the Buddha turns Sigala back toward the sunrise.

Honor your father and mother. Respect your elders. Listen to your teacher. Rules like these point one way: from the young to the old. The Sigalovada does something worth noticing. Every time it tells the young man what he owes, it turns around and says what is owed to him. Five duties going one way, five coming back, for parents and for teachers alike. A bow in two directions.
screen: `FROM THE YOUNG TO THE OLD.` → `FIVE DUTIES EACH WAY.` → `A BOW IN TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: East is the parents, the direction where the day begins. A child, the Buddha says, honors them in five ways, thinking: they supported me, so I'll support them. I'll do the work they need done. I'll keep up the family line. I'll be worthy of what they leave me. And when they've died, I'll make offerings in their memory. Parents, honored like this, show their love in five ways too. They keep their child from what's harmful, encourage what's good, have the child trained in a skill, help arrange a suitable marriage, and at the right time, hand over the inheritance. South is the teachers. A student honors a teacher by rising to greet them, by waiting on them, by being eager to learn, by small acts of service, and by taking the lesson seriously. The teacher in return trains the student well, makes sure they've really understood, teaches them the whole of the craft, speaks well of them to friends, and keeps them safe wherever they go. Notice the balance. The child's list ends with remembering parents after death; the parents' list ends with letting go of what they own at the right time. The student's list ends with attention; the teacher's with protection. Some details belong to ancient India, arranged marriages and inheritances. But the shape is plain. Respect flows up, care flows down, and when both flow, the direction is honored.
screen: `EAST: THEY SUPPORTED ME.` · `PARENTS: SKILL, MARRIAGE, INHERITANCE.` · `SOUTH: EAGER TO LEARN.` · `TEACHERS: THE WHOLE CRAFT, AND SAFETY.` · then, large: `EAST AND SOUTH.`

If you have children or students yourself, notice the duties coming back the other way.

571.title: West, north, below, above
571.hook: spouses, friends, workers, religious teachers: duties both ways
571.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists learn the Sigalovada's duties as a guide to marriage, friendship and work, and households support monastics with food and requisites while monastics teach and counsel in return.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents and teachers. Your line: respect flows up, care flows down. Today Sigala turns the rest of the way around, and the bow is complete.

Count the people behind an ordinary day. The person you live with. The friend who texted. The person who made your coffee, or cleaned the office, or delivered the package. Someone whose words you turn to when life gets heavy. Four kinds of people, and it's easy to thank only one or two of them. The last part of the Sigalovada finishes the circle: four more directions, four more pairs of duties.
screen: `THE PEOPLE BEHIND A DAY.` → `EASY TO THANK ONLY ONE OR TWO.` → `THE CIRCLE FINISHED.`

segments.voice: West is the spouse. The husband, in the sutta's world, honors his wife by respecting her, by never looking down on her, by being faithful, by giving her authority in the home, and by giving her gifts. She in return organizes the household well, is kind to both families and to the helpers, is faithful, protects what they've earned, and is skilled and tireless in her work. North is friends. You honor them by giving, by kind words, by helping, by treating them as equals, and by keeping your word. They in return look after you when you're careless, guard your things, are a refuge when you're afraid, don't leave you in trouble, and care about your family too. Below are those who work for you. You give them work suited to their strength, food and wages, care when they're sick, a share of special treats, and time off. They rise before you, rest after you, take only what's given, do good work, and speak well of you. Above are the spiritual teachers, the monks and brahmins of Sigala's day. You honor them with kindness in deed, word and thought, by keeping your door open to them, and by supplying their needs. They in return keep you from wrong, encourage what's good, care for you with a kind heart, teach you what you haven't heard, clarify what you have, and show you the way to a heavenly rebirth. Some details belong to their own century. Care in sickness and days off for workers still read as fresh. Six directions, and in each one, care going both ways.

572.title: So it isn't lost
572.hook: a teacher dies, his followers split, and Sariputta answers by counting
572.howItsDone: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions memorize texts and chant them together, and tradition says the Pali discourses were handed down by recitation for centuries before they were written down.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the circle of six directions, finished. Your line: every direction. Today, a new hall, a quarrel next door, and a plan so it doesn't happen here.

In the town of Pava, the local Mallas have just built a new meeting hall, so new that no teacher has used it yet. They invite the Buddha to be the first. He comes with his monks and talks with the townspeople late into the night. When they leave, his back aches. So he asks Sariputta, his senior student, to speak to the monks while he lies down on his right side, mindful. And Sariputta has news from town on his mind.
screen: `A NEW HALL IN PAVA.` → `A TEACHER WITH AN ACHING BACK.` → `SARIPUTTA SPEAKS INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Nigantha Nataputta, a well-known teacher of the time, the one Jains remember as Mahavira, has recently died here in Pava, and his followers, the discourse says, have split, arguing over what he really taught, wounding each other with words. Sariputta says, in effect: let's not let that happen to us. Let's recite the teaching together, all of us, in agreement, so this way of life lasts long, for the good of many. Then he does what you'd do if you wanted a whole room to remember. He counts. One thing: all beings are sustained by food. Two things: name and form. Three: the roots of harm, greed, hatred and delusion. Four: the foundations of mindfulness. On and on, all the way up to ten. It's the Sangiti Sutta, the reciting together. Tradition says the teaching wasn't written down for centuries; it lived in human memory, passed from mouth to ear. A number gives the mind a shelf: if you know there are four, you notice when you've only said three. Some scholars think lists like these were one way the early communities kept a huge body of teaching from drifting. And here's the quiet point. Sariputta's answer to a quarrel isn't a ruling on who was right. It's everyone saying the same words, together, out loud. At the end, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Sariputta, good.
screen: `A TEACHER DIES, A COMMUNITY SPLITS` · `LET'S RECITE IT TOGETHER` · `ONE, TWO, THREE, ALL THE WAY TO TEN` · `SAYING IT TOGETHER KEEPS THE PEACE` · then, large: `SO IT ISN'T LOST.`

segments.voice: Learn one short list by heart: the three roots of harm, greed, hatred, delusion, or the five precepts, no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. Say it once slowly, counting on your fingers, then again with your eyes closed, and rest on the breath. If it slips away later, that's fine: that's exactly why lists come with numbers.

573.title: By tens
573.hook: ten questions asked at every number, from one to ten
573.carry: what helps, what to let go
573.howItsDone: Many Buddhists learn the teaching through numbered lists, such as the four noble truths, the five precepts and the eightfold path, and monastic study in many countries still includes memorizing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta counting the teaching aloud. Your line: say it once more. Today he counts again, with a twist.

Any good mechanic has a checklist, even if it's only in their head. What's working? What needs attention? What has to come out? What would make this run better? Ask the same few questions of every part, and nothing gets missed. The thirty-fourth discourse, the last of the long ones, is built like that. Sariputta is speaking again, beside a lotus pond near the city of Champa. And instead of one list per number, he asks the same ten questions at every number, one through ten.
screen: `A MECHANIC'S CHECKLIST.` → `BESIDE A LOTUS POND IN CHAMPA.` → `TEN QUESTIONS AT EVERY NUMBER.`

segments.voice: It's the Dasuttara Sutta, roughly, going up to ten. Here's how it works. At number one, Sariputta asks: what one thing helps most? Diligence, care in doing good. What one thing should be developed? Mindfulness of the body, with gladness. What one thing should be fully understood? Contact, the meeting of the senses and the world, the kind that feeds clinging. What one thing should be let go? The conceit I am. What leads to decline? Careless attention. What leads to growth? Wise attention. And so on, ten questions in all, down to: what one thing should be realized? A freedom of mind that can't be shaken. Then he goes to two and asks all ten questions again, with two things for each answer. Then three, all the way to ten. Picture a grid: ten numbers down the side, ten questions across the top, every square filled. A whole way of life folded into a table. And the questions are practical. Not what's true about the universe, but what helps, what to grow, what to drop, what's slipping, what's getting better. Decline and growth often turn on the same thing done two ways: careless attention or wise attention. The Long Discourses end here, not with a story or a death scene, but with a teacher handing the community a tool to check itself, number by number.

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then name ten good things in your life right now, one finger at a time; small is fine, a warm cup, a friend's message, working knees, a window, a song. Let each one land before the next. When your hands are full, rest them in your lap and breathe with all ten.

574.title: Your long discourse
574.hook: of the long discourses, which one stays with you
574.howItsDone: Individual long discourses, such as the account of the Buddha's last days or the advice to Sigala, are read, chanted and taught on their own in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: by tens, Sariputta's grid of ten questions. Your line: what helps, what to let go. Today, the end of a week, and a question only you can answer.

Ask ten people who read the same novel what they remember, and you'll get ten different scenes. One remembers the storm. One, a line at a kitchen table. One, a side character nobody else noticed. Nine of them didn't read it wrong. A long book is a house with many rooms, and each reader ends up living in one. For seven weeks, this path has walked through the thirty-four Long Discourses. Kings, gods, wanderers, a courtesan, a skeptic prince, a young man bowing to the sky. Today adds nothing new.
screen: `TEN READERS, TEN SCENES.` → `A HOUSE WITH MANY ROOMS.` → `WHICH ROOM DO YOU LIVE IN?`

segments.voice: Some scenes, in case one is waiting for you. A king who killed his own father rides out under a full moon, asking what a spiritual life is good for, and hears that even a slave who goes forth would be honored by a king. A man builds a staircase to a palace he has never seen. A woman named Ambapali invites the Buddha to a meal, and when princes ask for the same day, he keeps his word to her. The Buddha, old and ill, tells Ananda there's no teacher's closed fist: nothing held back. Ananda weeps by a door, and the Buddha praises his long kindness as an attendant. A skeptical prince argues with a monk through story after story. And this week: young Sigala, bowing to six directions, learns what each bow could mean. Six ways wealth leaks away. How to tell a true friend. Duties that run both ways, between parents and children, teachers and students, spouses, friends, workers. Then Sariputta, counting so nothing is lost, and counting again by tens. In the last journey, the Buddha says that after he's gone, the teaching and the discipline will be the teacher. Not a person, not a successor: the words. And words do their work by being remembered. So the scene that stays with you isn't trivia. It's the teacher you actually took home, and it doesn't have to match anyone else's.
screen: `A MOONLIT KING, A STAIRCASE, A MEAL` · `THIS WEEK: SIGALA'S SIX DIRECTIONS` · `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER` · `THE SCENE THAT STAYED IS YOURS` · then, large: `YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let one scene from these weeks come up on its own, whichever arrives first, and walk into it slowly: where is it, what time of day, who is speaking, what does the air feel like? Stay inside it for a few breaths, the way you'd stand in a room you love. Then notice why this one came, without explaining it, and rest.
Digha Nikaya, the long collection: the one scene, out of thirty-four discourses, that stayed with you, the teaching you actually carried home. Today's word.
Your line: yours. One scene, carried home with you. A week done, day five hundred seventy-four.

chat.says: You read all thirty-four long Buddhist discourses? Which scene matters most?
options: The one that stays with you; the teaching itself is meant to be the teacher.
Only the first one; the rest just repeat it at greater length.
The longest one, since length shows which teaching mattered most.
chat.meaning: In DN 16 the Buddha says the teaching and discipline will be the teacher; the scene you remember is the teaching you carried home.
